# Review

## Summary

The note names only one proper noun: "Commonplace", in the heading of the
section that lists its mechanisms. The note never says what Commonplace is.
The listed mechanisms (titles, descriptions, indexes, link context, progressive
disclosure) imply a knowledge-base system. Even so, a first-time reader must
infer from those examples what kind of thing the name refers to, and whether
it is the host KB. A brief inline identification would resolve this. The note
names no other systems, tools, people or organizations.

# Review

## Summary

The title is a proposition, but its opposite ("a knowledge base should not support fluid resolution-switching") is not a position anyone informed would hold. "Fluid" already builds the desirability into the claim, which places it near the gate's `validation should be fast` failure example.

The body has a sharper point. It treats resolution-switching fluidity as a qualitative criterion that complements retrieval accuracy. It shows a system can retrieve the right detail yet make its wider context hard to recover, or offer an overview that never reaches the detail. It also separates the criterion from addressability grain, pointer accuracy and recall. A retrieval-focused designer could contest that independence claim, so it would make a stronger title. Alternatively, since the note mainly defines a term and inventories mechanisms, a topical title would also be valid under this gate.

# Review

The note is mostly compact. The four mechanism paragraphs each name a different
Commonplace surface and link to its support. The four questions turn the
criterion into checks that can be applied. The discovery section limits the
note's claim about recognition. The first Boundaries paragraph separates the
idea from addressability grain. Deleting any of these would make the note less
grounded or easier to misapply.

The redundancy is in the caveats. The note says it is qualitative and
task-relative in its opening. It says this again after the questions, then
again in the second Boundaries paragraph. The Open questions section covers
the same ground a fourth time. Each repeat is accurate, but each pre-empts a
misreading that an earlier sentence already rules out. That is the defensive
redundancy the criterion describes. Keeping the opening qualifier and the Open
questions, and adding "backlinks" to the third question's list of routes,
would keep everything these passages contribute in less space.

The sentence in the link-context paragraph about link relations and abstraction
is less clear-cut. It may answer a misreading specific to links, so it is
reported as INFO rather than WARN.

# Review

## Summary

The note explains its components well. Title-as-claim lets a reader inspect assertions before loading bodies. Link phrases carry why a target matters. Pointer tiers form a cost gradient. The contrast with retrieval accuracy names two concrete failure shapes: the right detail with no recoverable context, and an overview that never reaches detail.

The central claim itself is under-explained. The note does not state why a reader must alternate between views and cannot simply load what the task needs. It does not state what fluid switching buys that would be lost otherwise, beyond avoiding cost that is by definition avoidable. The task-relativity qualifiers in the opening and the Boundaries section accurately describe scope. Combined with the missing trade-off, though, they leave the prescription with no condition under which it would fail.

A hard-to-vary version would name the constraint that creates the need to switch. It would also say what the criterion forbids, such as a design that buys cheaper switching at a maintenance or context cost greater than the transitions it saves. The note's honest "qualitative criterion" framing limits how far this matters, so the finding is WARN, not FAIL.

# Review

## Summary

All links resolve to library notes in `kb/theory/`. Each was checked by reading its title and opening.

- **Title as claim enables traversal as reasoning.** The target says claim titles make the first disclosure layer usable, so agents can choose what to load. This supports "a reader can inspect a chain of assertions before choosing which bodies to load." Aligned.
- **Link-following and search impose different metadata requirements.** The target contrasts local steps that carry source context with long-range search that lacks it. The note uses the target only to say that both routes can take part in a switch. Aligned.
- **Link strength is encoded in position and prose.** This is a modest extension that is not articulated (WARN above).
- **Pointer design tradeoffs in progressive disclosure.** The target names exactly the four axes the note cites. It describes pointers "at increasing resolution", with cheap ones scanned first, which supports the cost gradient. Aligned.
- **Recognition, not linking, is the hard problem.** The target makes recognition the expensive step and requires co-presence. The note claims only that switching helps assemble views and "does not perform the recognition". Aligned and appropriately bounded.
- **Footer links.** These comprise agents-navigate, addressability grain and end-to-end evaluation. The note's one-sentence paraphrase of grain ("the smallest amount one access path can retrieve for a matched target") matches the target's definition. The other footer relations are adjacent and make no stronger support claim.

The only issue is the link-strength attribution.

# Review

Five body links were checked against their targets.

- "Because a [title-as-claim supports traversal as reasoning]": the target says claim titles make link traversal read as a chain of reasoning. The attribution holds.
- "Those routes have [different metadata requirements]": the target compares link-following and search as navigation modes with different metadata needs. The attribution holds.
- "[pointer types trade off specificity, cost, availability, and accuracy]": the target names context-specificity, cost, availability and accuracy as its four axes and describes progressive disclosure as pointers at increasing resolution. The attribution holds.
- "[Recognizing shared structure] requires more than navigation": the target defines recognition as seeing shared structure and treats it as the expensive step. The attribution holds.
- "This is the navigational value of [encoding link strength in position and prose]": the target is about link weight and traversal priority, not about preserving bearings during a resolution switch. This is the one finding.

The footer links state relations rather than concept identities. Their glosses agree with the target heads.

# Friction check: A knowledge base should support fluid resolution-switching

**Central claim (one sentence):** A knowledge base should let a reader move between broader and narrower views, in whichever direction the task needs, at low transition cost and without losing why the views belong together.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The properties held at once are low transition cost in both directions, no loading of unrelated material, preserved relationship between views, and task-relativity, including permission for routes other than outbound links. These can coexist. Richer link context and intermediate views add some reading cost, but they do so to avoid larger avoidable costs, and the note asks only for avoidable cost to be removed. The hedge "task-relevant" reconciles "in both directions" with "Nor does every task need to return to a broad view". So the claim concretizes to one consistent criterion, though it is weak: it is qualitative and offers no scoring rule, as the note says.

## Thinnest joints

The weakest joint is the opening normative step to the upward direction, because the note gives no reason for it beyond observing that readers alternate. It also leaves unresolved whether the artifact or the system supplies the route back. The two mechanism paragraphs come next. Each one supports the downward, narrowing move well, and each is then credited with the bidirectional, scope-crossing property the criterion defines. This is where the note's fluent prose covers a gap. The contrast with retrieval accuracy is half supported. The title-as-claim inference is the strongest joint and holds within its stated scope. The discovery and grain-boundary paragraphs are hedged enough that they make no load-bearing inference worth surfacing.

## For the human
Look first at the upward direction. Say under what entry conditions, such as arrival by search versus descent from an index, a route back is needed, and whether the artifact or the system owes it. The link-context and progressive-disclosure mechanisms currently mostly support downward movement.

# Critique: A knowledge base should support fluid resolution-switching

**Note:** kb/theory/a-knowledge-base-should-support-fluid-resolution-switching.md
**Central commitment:** A knowledge base should make task-relevant movement among broad and detailed views inexpensive in both directions, and this "resolution-switching fluidity" is a qualitative evaluative criterion distinct from, and complementary to, retrieval accuracy, addressability grain and pointer accuracy.
**Critique mode:** claim (with a definitional component: the criterion's distinctness from existing properties is load-bearing)
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

This objection comes from an evaluation reductionist: the information-retrieval and component-metric tradition, or within this KB the end-to-end evaluation note's own method of keeping separate diagnostics "without inventing a total score". A new criterion earns its place only if it predicts failures that existing component measures miss. "Resolution-switching fluidity" does not meet that test, for two reasons.

**First, each diagnostic question reduces to an existing property.**

- Q1 asks whether the reader can choose a narrower target without opening every body. The pointer-design and "agents navigate by deciding what to read next" notes already cover this as pointer specificity and accuracy at a follow-or-skip decision.
- Q2 asks whether the reader can reach the detail without loading unrelated material. This is the addressability grain note's matched selective-read floor, almost word for word: "retrieve through the access path in use without loading the rest of the artifact."
- Q3 asks whether the reader can recover a broader view by link, index or search. That is route availability: backlinks, index membership and search coverage.
- Q4 asks whether the transition preserves why the two views belong together. The link-strength note's contextual articulation covers this.

The note's own Commonplace mechanisms section confirms the mapping. Every mechanism it lists is borrowed from one of those linked notes. The "complements retrieval accuracy" contrast then knocks down a narrower opponent than the one that exists. The linked end-to-end note already rejects evaluation by retrieval alone and lists "navigation or decision cost" among its diagnostics.

**Second, once the criterion is hedged, its "should" loses observable content.** The note says:

- fluidity is relative to the task and to the operations available;
- only *avoidable* transition cost counts;
- not every task needs to return to a broad view;
- an outward route may come from search instead of an authored link;
- no scoring rule or threshold exists.

What remains is: make the transitions a task needs no more expensive than they must be. No designer rejects that. Under this reading, the title's normative claim either restates generic cost minimization or names a conjunction of properties the KB already has notes for. The author cannot dismiss this in one sentence, because the note's best defence, "none alone establishes bidirectional navigability", concedes the reductionist's point that a conjunction might.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.**

- The Boundaries section separates the criterion from addressability grain, pointer accuracy and retrieval recall. Its grain contrast, in which grain prices the smallest retrievable unit while resolution-switching asks whether views at different scopes exist and connect, is a real distinction. A KB could have fine grain and no broad views at all. That is the strongest part of the defence, and it keeps the attack from landing fully.
- The evaluative criterion section gives two concrete failure cases: right detail with an unrecoverable wider context, and an overview that never reaches detail.
- The section explicitly limits the criterion to "a qualitative design criterion, not yet a metric". The open questions concede that it has no cost unit and no dead-end test.

What the note does not engage:

- **The conjunction.** It argues against each component property *alone*, not against their combination, so the reduction stays open.
- **Q2 and grain.** It never notices that its second diagnostic question restates grain, which undercuts the boundary it draws.
- **The wider baseline.** Both failure cases are framed against retrieval accuracy, not against the end-to-end diagnostic set the note links to.
- **Vacuity.** It does not show a design choice that the criterion would reject and that the existing measures would accept.

The surviving part of the attack is this: as written, the criterion is defensible as a named, transition-level view over existing properties. It is not yet shown to be an independent property with its own failure mode.

## Constructive findings

- Supply one separating case: a KB, or a Commonplace configuration, where pointer accuracy, grain, recall, upward-route availability and link context each pass, yet a task still pays avoidable transition cost. Possible sources are the absence of intermediate views between a topic index and note bodies, or a broad view whose groupings do not match the task's decomposition. If no such case exists, restate the commitment as a named bundle that evaluates these properties together at transitions. That is a weaker but honest claim.
- Rewrite Q2 so it asks what grain does not: whether a route exists from the current broad view into the needed unit. Alternatively, credit grain for Q2 and keep only the transition-specific remainder.
- Give the "should" observable content by naming one design the criterion rejects, for example detail artifacts reachable only by search, with no index or backlink, for a task that repeatedly re-orients. State why the existing diagnostics would not flag it.
- Compare the criterion with the end-to-end note's diagnostic set, not with retrieval accuracy alone, and say which transition failure that set misses.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- Treating "resolution" as task-relative view scope instead of artifact abstraction rank is reasonable. However, the term invites a reading of fixed levels, such as zoom levels or abstraction tiers. The disclaimer appears only once, in the opening paragraph. Later uses of "broad" and "detailed" quietly rely on a fairly stable ordering of index above note above body.
- The connection-to-discovery section is careful to say that switching does not perform recognition. It gives no mechanism by which fluid switching *raises* the chance of recognition, so its contribution to the note's case is mostly a disclaimer.

# Premise decomposition: A knowledge base should support fluid resolution-switching

**Register:** claim
**Central commitment (one sentence):** A knowledge base should make task-relevant transitions between broader and narrower views inexpensive in both directions while preserving why the views belong together, and this qualitative criterion is distinct from and complementary to retrieval accuracy.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment is a normative design criterion with two parts: a definitional cut (what resolution-switching is and what it is not) and a "should" that is bidirectional. It consumes three kinds of premise. First, descriptive premises about reading: readers do alternate between scopes, and switch cost is separable from retrieval accuracy. Both hold, partly because the note already fences the obvious exceptions with "task-relevant" and its Boundaries section. Second, mechanism premises: that titles, descriptions, indexes, link phrases and progressive disclosure supply the views and preserve the relationships between them. The pointer-gradient premise survives because it is stated conditionally. The link-context premise is dented: authored phrases carry the author's argument, not the reader's task. Third, premises the "should" consumes without stating them. The downward and upward directions must both discriminate between designs, and providing the routes must be worth its cost. The upward direction is weakened by the note's own concession that search counts as a route back, which makes that half nearly vacuous unless the "preserves why" question carries it. The cost premise is never stated, and maintenance drift is a concrete way switch routes become misleading.

No premise failure propagates to the commitment as a whole. The criterion is modest and explicitly qualitative, so each dent can be repaired by a qualification in the Boundaries section rather than by retracting the claim.

## For the human

Look first at the upward-route premise: once search counts as a route back, decide whether the "back" half of "both directions" is tested by the fourth question (preserved relationship) and say so, or the bidirectional criterion stops distinguishing designs.

# Simplification synthesis: A knowledge base should support fluid resolution-switching

The note is compact, and its central claim appears early. Three of the four
checks passed. The remaining value is structural: the scope caveats are spread
across the note, and the full criterion is stated only in the middle. The
abstraction caveat in the link-context paragraph, which two checks flagged as
INFO, is a one-sentence local trim. It falls below this synthesis's threshold.

## Opportunities

### 1. Consolidate the qualitative and task-relative caveats

- Location: opening, "This is a qualitative design criterion, not yet a metric
  or a claim that every task needs the same sequence of views"; The evaluative
  criterion, "These questions identify possible friction. They do not yet supply
  a scoring rule or universal threshold."; the second paragraph of Boundaries,
  "An artifact does not need an outbound link in every case. … Fluidity is
  relative to the task and to the navigation operations actually available to
  the reader."; and the second Open question.
- Combines: both WARN findings from marginal-value-redundancy (the post-question
  caveat and the second Boundaries paragraph).
- Reader problem: the same limitation appears four times. A reader cannot tell
  whether each repeat adds a new restriction, and the section ends in caveats
  rather than in the distinction from neighbouring concepts.
- Direction: keep the opening qualifier as the single statement of status and
  task-relativity. Add backlinks to the third question's routes ("an authored
  link, index, backlinks, or search"). Delete the post-question sentence and the
  second Boundaries paragraph. Boundaries would then hold only the distinctions
  from grain, pointer accuracy and retrieval recall.
- Preserve or decide: two phrases may carry points the opening does not quite
  cover. The author should decide whether to fold them into the opening or let
  them go. "Universal threshold" says more than "not yet a metric": a metric
  could still exist without one fixed cutoff. "Nor does every task need to return
  to a broad view after reading detail" qualifies the bidirectional claim
  itself, not just the sequence of views. If the author means the "both
  directions" requirement as a capability the KB offers rather than a path every
  task follows, that should stay explicit near the opening claim. The second Open
  question assumes the reader already knows that search or backlinks can supply
  the outward route, so the third question must name them once the Boundaries
  paragraph is gone.

### 2. State the full criterion in the opening

- Location: The evaluative criterion, "**Resolution-switching fluidity** asks
  whether a reader can move among the views a task needs without paying
  avoidable transition cost or losing the relationship between them", compared
  with the opening's second paragraph, "A knowledge base should make
  task-relevant switches inexpensive in both directions."
- Combines: the INFO finding from core-claim-obscured.
- Reader problem: the opening gives the cost condition and the return route,
  but not the condition that the transition keeps the relationship between views.
  That condition appears first in the link-context paragraph and is stated as
  part of the criterion only after the inventory, under a newly coined term.
  So the reader assembles the claim in stages and meets two labels for one idea.
- Direction: add the relationship condition to the second opening paragraph,
  so the claim reads as cheap transitions that keep their relationship. The
  criterion section could then introduce the four questions directly and not
  restate the criterion under a new name. One possible resolution, offered only
  as an illustration: "A knowledge base should make task-relevant switches
  inexpensive in both directions without losing why the two views belong
  together."
- Preserve or decide: decide whether "resolution-switching fluidity" names a
  distinct concept, an evaluative property of the KB as opposed to the reader's
  operation, or just restates the title's "fluid". If it is distinct, keep the
  term and define it in the opening. If not, reuse "resolution-switching". The
  link-context paragraph and the fourth question both rely on the relationship
  condition, so it is part of the note's claim and must survive any compression
  of the opening.

# Role in the KB: A knowledge base should support fluid resolution-switching

## Role
The note supplies the term "resolution-switching" — movement between broad and narrow views of a KB — that three theory notes and three source ingests cite when they talk about breadth versus depth of reading. Theory dependents use it as an extension target: pointer tiers form its gradient, title-scanning versus full loading are its two modes, and areas sit among its levels. Ingests cite it as the concept their sources give evidence for. No dependent argues from the note's evaluative criterion or its boundaries.
Relied on: the term resolution-switching and its definition as movement among broad and narrow views; the titles/descriptions/bodies breadth–depth mechanism; the progressive-disclosure cost gradient of pointer tiers; link context preserving relationships across a switch. Unused: the four-question evaluative criterion, "resolution-switching fluidity" as a named criterion, the complement to retrieval accuracy, the boundary with addressability grain, pointer accuracy and recall, the outbound-link-not-required boundary, the link-following/search distinction, and the open questions on measurement.
